overview:
On the night of 24 April 1915, Ottoman police in Constantinople arrested several hundred Armenian writers, clergy, teachers and political figures — the beginning of a campaign that within two years emptied Anatolia of a population that had lived there for millennia. The empire was at war, reeling from defeat against Russia in the Caucasus, and the ruling Committee of Union and Progress treated its Armenian subjects as an internal enemy. A Temporary Law of Deportation passed in late May authorised the military to remove populations from any area it deemed a security risk, and the removals quickly extended far beyond the front, reaching communities a thousand miles from any fighting. Able-bodied men were separated out and killed at the edge of town. The remainder — women, children, the old — were marched south toward the Syrian desert and the camps around Deir ez-Zor, where starvation, thirst, disease and attacks by gendarmes, irregulars of the paramilitary Special Organization, and local militias did what the marches had not. A second round of killings in 1916 finished off much of what remained. Estimates of the dead vary with the method and the archive: the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum gives at least 664,000 and possibly 1.2 million out of a prewar Armenian population of roughly 1.5 million, while other scholars work with figures approaching or exceeding a million.

Death was not the only mechanism. Somewhere between 100,000 and 200,000 Armenians, overwhelmingly women and children, were absorbed into Muslim households and state orphanages through abduction, forced marriage and conversion — survival purchased at the price of identity. Property left behind was redistributed under a succession of "abandoned properties" laws, a transfer of land, workshops, houses and capital so large that historians such as Taner Akçam and Umit Kurt argue the economic foundations of the Turkish Republic rest partly on it. Armed resistance was rare and rarely effective. Ottoman Armenians were scattered, disarmed and led by figures who mostly counselled compliance; of the hundreds of communities ordered out, only a handful fought. The three events this map holds beneath the story are among them. At Musa Dagh, villagers from six settlements near the Mediterranean coast refused the deportation order in July 1915, withdrew up the mountain with a few hundred rifles, and held out fifty-three days until French warships spotted their signal banners and evacuated more than four thousand people to Port Said — the one case where Allied intervention saved a whole community. At Urfa that August, the resistance lasted twenty-five days before German-assisted Ottoman forces broke it and killed most of the population. At Azakh in the southeast, mainly Assyrian defenders with some Armenians among them held a siege from August to November 1915, a reminder that the same machinery consumed Assyrian and Greek Christians as well.

The killing did not stop with the armistice. Ottoman courts-martial in 1919–1920 tried some organisers and sentenced several in absentia, but the prosecutions collapsed as the Kemalist national movement gained ground, and the survivors who tried to return home found the process running in reverse. When Kemalist forces took Smyrna in September 1922 and fire swept the Christian quarters, the last substantial Armenian and Greek populations of Anatolia left by sea. The Republic of Turkey was proclaimed the following year, which is why the story's span closes in 1923: not because the violence had a formal end, but because by then there was almost nobody left to remove.
significance: This was the case that taught the twentieth century what a modern state could do to its own citizens with paperwork, railways and telegraph orders, and Raphael Lemkin cited it explicitly among the crimes that drove him to coin the word "genocide" in 1944. It also became the founding case of organised denial: Turkey has maintained for a century that the deportations were a wartime security measure and the figures inflated, destroyed or sealed relevant records, and pressured foreign governments and even Hollywood studios into silence — which in turn made recognition a live diplomatic question in dozens of parliaments well into the 2020s. For Armenians the consequence was a diaspora rather than a homeland: the communities of Anatolia never reformed, and the memory of 1915 became the organising fact of Armenian identity from Beirut to Los Angeles.
coverage: Written from the Wikipedia synthesis, the USHMM encyclopedia, the Armenian National Institute, and the Wikipedia survey of Armenian self-defense; the death toll, the number forcibly converted, and the boundaries of the 1915–1923 span are all genuinely contested rather than merely rounded, and the Ottoman documentary base is incomplete because records were destroyed at the time and property archives reclassified as state secrets in 2006. The dataset holds only three events, all of them armed defenses, which badly skews the picture — resistance was the exception, and the deportation routes, the Deir ez-Zor camps, the 24 April arrests and the Smyrna endpoint that constitute the main story are not represented here. Azakh in particular was primarily an Assyrian episode and sits under this story somewhat awkwardly.
